title: Reseat a chrome wire shelf's dropped front corner whose split sleeve has slipped a groove down its post
instruction: The front right corner of the middle shelf has dropped. Put it back level with the other three corners.
context: Chrome wire shelving (Metro Super Erecta and its many consumer copies) stands in garages, pantries, closets and stockrooms. Each shelf corner has a tapered collar. The collar wedges over a plastic split sleeve, and the sleeve's two halves snap round a 1-inch post at one of its grooves, spaced 1 inch apart. If a sleeve is not seated in its groove, it slides down under load. One corner then sits a groove low and the shelf twists, so items roll toward that corner. Pushing the corner up does not fix it, because the sleeve stays low and the collar falls back. Someone has to hold the corner above the right groove, close both sleeve halves round the post there, and then lower the collar onto them. This category does not need an occupation size. Owners do this themselves; makers sell helper tools and aluminium sleeves because the sleeves slip.
real_product: Metro (InterMetro) Super Erecta: 1424NC chrome wire shelf, 14 x 24 in, listed at 5.5 lb (2.5 kg) with an 800 lb capacity (KaTom https://www.katom.com/001-1424NC.html; WebstaurantStore 4611424NC). SiteSelect posts (13P and longer lines such as 27P) are 1 in in diameter, grooved every 1 in and numbered every 2 in (Metro wire-shelving manual quoted by search; 13P listings at tequipment.net/Metro/13P and webstaurantstore 46113P). The 9985 split sleeve is 1.75 in tall and 1.25 in wide, sold "4 pairs per bag" with one bag per shelf (https://metro.com/shop/metro-replacement-plastic-split-sleeves-for-super-erecta-industrial-wire-shelving-pack-of-4). Each sleeve is therefore two loose halves. Metro's wording is "tapered openings in the shelf corners slide over the tapered split sleeves providing a positive lock". Generic assembly sheets (WebstaurantStore's Steelton and wire_shelving_installation_guide PDFs, both read) say: "(4) Pairs of Sleeves per Shelf"; "Snap the sleeves onto the grooves on each post. Ensure that the small, tapered side of each sleeve is facing up"; "Press down on each corner ... rubber mallet". The fault is real: a Thingiverse helper notes that "split plastic shelf support sleeves may slip downward causing the shelf to be uneven", and reviewers of aluminium sleeves say they stopped the slipping. The product keeps both the fault and the forced skill. The blocker is the sleeve itself: it is two loose halves that a person holds round the post in one hand, thumb again
fault: The scene is a 3-shelf Metro unit with 1424 shelves on 27P posts, standing on the table. At the middle shelf, the front-right sleeve has its rib in the groove one below the other three, 25.4 mm lower. That corner's collar is wedged on it, so the corner sits 25 mm low and the shelf is twisted. In a rigid-body simulation, a one-piece shelf cannot twist: with one support low, it rocks on its diagonal instead. Getting the true twisted state needs the shelf modelled as two triangles hinged along the B-D diagonal, with an estimated torsion spring.
skill: The left arm approaches from the front and pinches the shelf's 1 in front truss with its fingers vertical, 16 to 20 cm in from the post. It lifts the corner about 5 cm against the shelf's weight and twist, then holds it there. The right arm also approaches from the front with its fingers along y. It opens the low sleeve, then closes both halves round the post at the groove above, with each rib in the groove. The left arm then lowers the corner so the collar wedges on the sleeve, and both arms withdraw. Unloading the cans first is allowed and does not remove the hold-and-fit, because the empty shelf still needs it. The step a parallel gripper cannot do: it can hold only one loose half against the post, never both together. The holding arm cannot help without dropping the corner.
nearest:
I grepped pipeline/known_tasks.tsv (2,479 rows) for: shelf, shelv, shelving, sleeve, collar, post, split, wedge, taper, clip, corner, groove, bracket, pin, wire, chrome, leg, dropped, sag and slipped. I also ran gh PR searches for "wire shelving", "split sleeve", "shelving post", "Metro shelf", shelving and sleeve, and grepped pipeline/concepts, claims, candidates and novelty-reviews. No task covers wire shelving, Super Erecta or a post sleeve. The nearest PRs, with their review comments where I read them:

- **#941, split spacer halves round a captive shaft:** Not accepted, final. Ruled a variant of the same team's fork placement: "placing two spacer halves around the captive shaft repeats the earlier task's core skill". #179 is its withdrawn earlier copy.
- **#1221, level a rack shelf by moving one pull pin:** final. Rejected as a miniature ("13 cm-high rack and 0.4 kg shelf") and as not core stocker work.
- **#1946, gondola shelf brackets and steel shelf:** final, "significantly simplified compared to the cited real-world context".
- **#1244, dumbbell collars:** final. "Ordinary ring placement", and the collars did not grip.
- **#1902, roll a cabinet shelf through its face frame onto four pins:** accepted. It differs: no sleeve, and nothing to hold while working.
- **#1663, folding table leg brace ring over the knee:** accepted after being moved to Societal relatability. That is a ring slid along a leg; ours is two halves closed round a post while the load is held.
- **Our own work:** #2406 (shower chair, pending) has the same "one of four supports is one index low; lift that corner and re-index it" shape, and a rigid sim shelf would rock on its diagonal just as that chair does. Also our final rejection #2398 (board missed support) and tasks/reseat-shelf-prop-under-load.

Because of #2406, the "variant of one of our own" risk is real, even though the fitting step differs (snapping split halves rather than pressing a button).
reach_check:
I ran ik.solve offline with the real arm bases (0, ±0.305, 0.75), table top 0.7475 and 6 to 8 seeds per pose. Controls and posts stayed at their real places: a 27P unit with near posts at x 0.32, y ±0.286 and the middle shelf seated at table + 0.33 m.

Top-down grips fail at this height:
- Right-arm pinch at the post, pressing on the collar: 40.8 mm / 35°.
- Left-arm front-edge hold: 179 to 260 mm.
- Right arm holding the edge: 35 to 42 mm.

Front approaches all reach:
- **Sleeve pinch, right arm:** gripper pointing +x, fingers along y, at (0.32, -0.286), z table + 0.305, 0.33 and 0.39 (slipped groove, target groove, and above). Error 0.02 mm / 0.00°, within limits, joint margin 0.65 rad. At 60° and 75° pitch it was 0.02 to 0.03 mm.
- **Corner hold, left arm:** front approach, fingers vertical (roll ±90°), pinching the front truss 10, 16 or 20 cm in from the post, at seated height and 6 cm lifted. Error 0.01 to 0.04 mm / 0.01°, within limits.
- **Pick from the bottom shelf, right arm:** a dropped half at (0.40, -0.20, table + 0.165), top-down (0.04 mm, but only 0.05 rad joint margin) or at 45° (0.02 mm).

The right arm cannot approach from the outside of the post (62 to 68 mm error). So both arms must work at one corner with their grippers only 10 to 20 cm apart in y. Reach is not the blocker; holding the sleeve halves is (see risks).
reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. Kill: build=false. In order of severity:

1. **The forced skill cannot be done with parallel grippers on the real hardware.** A Metro 9985 sleeve is two loose half-shells. A person holds both round the post in one hand while the other hand holds the corner up. A parallel gripper can press only one half against the post, and the other arm is already holding the shelf. Every simulated workaround changes the mechanism: a one-piece ring that clicks from groove to groove, a half that clips itself on by a joint lock, or a fake third support. Reviewers rejected exactly this kind of change in #2379 and #2383 (altered hardware to suit the gripper), and we would expect the same here.
2. **A rigid shelf cannot twist.** One low corner makes a one-piece shelf rock on its diagonal, which turns this into our pending shower chair (#2406): one support one index short, lift the corner, re-index it. That invites a "variant of your own task" rejection. Avoiding it needs a two-triangle hinged shelf with an estimated torsion spring, which also has to be disclosed.
3. **Simulation physics would be fragile.** It needs a tapered collar wedging on thin tapered shells in PhysX with friction 1.2, ribs in 1 mm grooves, and a snap to model. Interpenetration and jitter are likely. The wedge also has no elastic preload, so the 0.5 partial-credit state may never occur.
4. **Importance is only moderate.** Societal relatability is plausible, since wire shelving is in tens of millions of homes, but a strict reviewer may call reseating one slipped corner occasional upkeep. The jobs angle (stockers, cooks) fails as not core work, as #1221 shows.
5. **Similar skill already judged.** #941 rejected closing split halves round a shaft as not distinct, though that ruling was about a same-team variant.
6. **Load and payload.** Holding the corner means lifting part of a 2.5 kg shelf plus any cans, and the arm's payload is not documented in the simulator package. Cans have to be allowed off without penalty, which makes the load decorative.

What would rescue it: a real one-piece hinged or clip-on sleeve product that one gripper can close round a post, plus a reviewer ruling that a sleeve fault is distinct from the shower chair. I found neither.
